newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: No more frenzied work days for Ramos, say doctors.
newsitem.headline: No more frenzied work days for Ramos, say doctors.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos may never be able to return to his frenzied lifestyle and 18-hour work days after an operation on Monday to remove an arterial block in his neck, doctors said.
It was the first sign of mortality in the energetic 68-year-old, who is somewhat of a legend for his lengthy work schedules, a passion for golf and an inclination to cut loose on the dance floor.

Doctors detected all was not well with the former army general about 10 days ago when he checked into hospital complaining of pains in his joints only hours after telling businessmen he had "enormous" staying power.
"He cannot follow his old schedule, it was too strenuous," Ramos's doctor, Raul Fores, said after a cholesterol blockage the size of a bean was surgically removed from a major artery in his neck.
"For the first time, he has listened (to doctors' advice). He realises he's got to slow down."
Until now, Ramos has been known in the Philippines as a man without a Sunday in his calendar.

He uses two alarm clocks to ensure he is up every day at 4:30 in the morning, his wife Amelita has said. Often, he would leave his bodyguards panting for breath as he rushed from one engagement to another. Working until midnight was common.

But carelessness about what he ate, perhaps "too much cheese and chocolates", and the stressful lifestyle led to the cholesterol build-up, Fores said. He said the president suffered from "the usual problems of people above 60".
Addressing businessmen on December 10, Ramos said: "My stamina or staying power, I must confess to you, is enormous."
Hours later, aides were driving him to hospital for the first of a series of checks that culminated in Monday's surgery.

"His (Ramos's) age is a negative factor for him but he is very athletic. From an outside point of view, his recovery should be faster than that of an ordinary person," said heart specialist Nelson Abelardo.
But Abelardo also added the president needed to slow down. "If you continue to drive yourself to perform to higher levels, soooner or later, something will have to give way," he said.
Abelardo, who is not a member of Ramos's medical team, said the ailment that struck Ramos possibly could recur, "but if the block is totally removed, that can take years to happen".
Without the surgery, the blockage might have left Ramos susceptible eventually to a stroke, other doctors said.
"If it is a major blockage, it can knock your brain out and cause a massive stroke," said one specialist, speaking anonymously.
